correctness.rationale: For i<=j-2 the record and peak use disjoint observations; for i>=j+2 the insertion rank determining the record is independent of the preceding internal order, which determines the peak. On the three remaining diagonals the respective joint probabilities are 1/((j-1)(j+1)), 1/(j+1) and zero. For the first probability, given R_(j-1), the first j-1 maximum has density (j-1)x^(j-2), and the two new observations produce a peak at j with probability (1-x^2)/2 conditional on this maximum. The second joint event is precisely that the first j+1 maximum occurs at j; the third is impossible. Subtracting 1/(3i) gives the frozen kernel, including the zero at j=2,i=1. The column sum is 1/(3j(j-1)(j+1)); partial fractions telescope to the stated total. The independent insertion ranks give the record variance. For two peaks at lag two, conditioning on the shared observation x yields joint probability integral_0^1 ((1-x^2)/2)^2 dx=2/15 and covariance 1/45; lag one is incompatible and greater lags are independent. Summing gives peak variance 2(n+1)/45 for n>=4 and the separate 2/9 at n=3. The claimed correlation and its asymptotic then follow with the stated n>=4 convention.
residual_risks: The uploaded script was inspected, not executed. The separate exhaustive finite check concerns sizes 3–8 only; the all-size result rests on the proof.
The model excludes endpoint peaks and ties; the correlation formula using 2(n+1)/45 starts at n=4.

value.rationale: As mathematical content the complete position-resolved law is structurally useful for mixed second moments of weighted sums of two classical permutation statistics. It identifies pairwise independence off the three diagonals and an exact cancellation within every column that accounts for the order-one total. This is value of the full structural result, not an independent value claim for routine correlation normalization or for duplicating the indexed theorem.
residual_risks: Pairwise independence off the diagonals does not imply independence of the vectors or a higher-order mixed law.
